title: Ontario will soon require licence, registration, insurance for e-bikes
summary: Some e-bike drivers will soon have to get a driver’s licence, vehicle registration and insurance to ride on Ontario's roads, Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria announced Wednesday.

blocks.text: Some e-bike drivers will soon have to get a driver’s licence, vehicle registration and insurance to ride on Ontario's roads, Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria announced Wednesday.
Province to require licence, registration, insurance for e-bikes that don't meet list of requirements
Ontario imposing new e-bike regulations from May 1, 2027
Come spring, some e-bike drivers will have to get a driver’s licence, vehicle registration and insurance to ride on Ontario's roads.
Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria announced Thursday that the province is tightening regulations on motorcycle- and motorscooter-style e-bikes, citing safety concerns.
"Simply putting pedals on a motorcycle doesn’t make it a bicycle," said Sarkaria at a news conference.
"If a vehicle looks and operates like a motorcycle, it needs to follow the rules for a motorcycle. It’s that simple."

Toronto police cracking down on e-bikes, e-scooters evading laws, regulations

blocks.text: Starting May 1, e-bikes in Ontario must have exposed bicycle-style frames, maximum motor-assisted speed of 32 km/h, and maximum power output of 500 watts.
The new regulations also divide e-bikes into two classes, each with maximum weight limits of 55 kilograms and 120 kilograms.
Vehicles that do not meet the requirements need to meet licensing, registration and insurance requirements to be on the roads.
People who violate the regulation will face fines of up to $2,500 and vehicle impoundment.

blocks.text: Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow welcomed the regulations, saying it’s necessary for safety.
"We want to encourage people to not necessarily drive. Use other modes of transportation, but do it safely," said Chow at an unrelated news conference Thursday morning.
As of Nov. 22, police enforcement involving e-bikes has increased by 106 per cent this year compared to the same period last year, according to Toronto police Supt. Mandeep Mann.
There have been 909 reported collisions involving micromobility devices, including 364 involving e-bikes during the same period, Mann said.
